title: Sentence variety & combining
examples: When should I use a semicolon instead of a comma?
What is the difference between combining with 'and' versus using a relative clause?
Can I combine too many sentences in one paragraph?

explain.say: Today we are looking at making your writing more interesting. We will learn how to combine short sentences into longer, flowing ones.
One way to combine sentences is using coordinating conjunctions. These words join two equal ideas together. Think of words like and, but, or.

draw.text: FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So

explain.say: Another technique is using subordinating conjunctions. These words show a relationship like time or cause. Examples include because or although.
We can also combine sentences using relative pronouns. These words add extra detail about a noun. We use words like who or which.
In everyday life, you combine ideas when you write an email. You might start with a greeting and then explain your main point clearly.
A common mistake is using a comma splice. This happens when you join two full sentences with only a comma. Remember you need more than just a comma.

items: Incorrect: I ran fast, I missed the bus.
Correct: I ran fast, so I missed the bus.

faq.q: What is the difference between a comma and a semicolon?
faq.a: A comma joins words or small phrases. A semicolon joins two complete, related sentences that could stand alone.
asks: When do I use a semicolon?
Can I use a semicolon instead of a period?

faq.q: Do I always need to combine my sentences?
faq.a: No, sometimes short, punchy sentences are best for impact. However, varying your length keeps the reader engaged.
asks: Is it bad to have short sentences?
When is it okay to keep sentences separate?

faq.a: Both mean a cause, but 'because' often introduces the main reason, while 'since' can sometimes suggest time. They are often interchangeable.

faq.q: How do I know if two sentences are equal in length?
faq.a: If you can put a period after the first sentence and it still makes perfect sense, they are likely equal ideas.
asks: How do I check if a sentence is complete?

faq.q: Is combining sentences always better for writing?
faq.a: It depends on your goal. If you want excitement, short sentences work. If you want flow, combining is useful.
asks: Does combining make my writing sound complicated?

facts: Coordinating conjunctions connect two independent clauses.
Subordinating conjunctions introduce a dependent clause.
Relative pronouns like who and which add descriptive detail.
A comma splice occurs when only a comma joins two full sentences.

quiz.say: The rain stopped, and the children ran outside.
quiz.show: The rain stopped, and the children ran outside.

options.show: The rain stopped, and the children ran outside.
options.say: The rain stopped, and the children ran outside.

options.show: The rain stopped and the children ran outside.
options.say: The rain stopped and the children ran outside.

options.show: Because the rain stopped, the children ran outside.
options.say: Because the rain stopped, the children ran outside.

options.show: The rain stopped; the children ran outside.
options.say: The rain stopped; the children ran outside.

quiz.why: This correctly uses the comma before the coordinating conjunction 'and' to join two equal ideas.

wrong.1: You need a comma before the conjunction when joining two full sentences.
wrong.2: This changes the meaning to suggest the stopping rain was the only reason they ran.
wrong.3: While a semicolon is possible, 'and' shows a clearer connection of related actions here.

quiz.say: She studied hard, so she passed the difficult exam.
quiz.show: She studied hard, so she passed the difficult exam.

options.show: She studied hard; she passed the difficult exam.
options.say: She studied hard; she passed the difficult exam.

options.show: Since she studied hard she passed the difficult exam.
options.say: Since she studied hard she passed the difficult exam.

options.show: She studied hard, so she passed the difficult exam.
options.say: She studied hard, so she passed the difficult exam.

options.show: She studied hard so she passed the difficult exam.
options.say: She studied hard so she passed the difficult exam.

quiz.why: The comma and the coordinating conjunction 'so' correctly show cause and effect between two main ideas.

wrong.0: Using only a semicolon suggests the ideas are related but doesn't show the clear result.
wrong.1: This is missing necessary punctuation to separate the introductory dependent clause.
wrong.3: You must place a comma before the coordinating conjunction 'so' when joining two full sentences.

quiz.say: The book, which was very old, smelled dusty.
quiz.show: The book, which was very old, smelled dusty.

options.show: The book was very old, so it smelled dusty.
options.say: The book was very old, so it smelled dusty.

options.show: The book, which was very old, smelled dusty.
options.say: The book, which was very old, smelled dusty.

options.show: The book which was very old smelled dusty.
options.say: The book which was very old smelled dusty.

options.show: The book which was very old, smelled dusty.
options.say: The book which was very old, smelled dusty.

quiz.why: Using commas around 'which was very old' correctly sets off non-essential, descriptive information.

wrong.0: This changes the meaning to suggest the age caused the smell, which might not be the intended meaning.
wrong.2: Omitting the commas makes the description sound like it is essential to identifying the book.
wrong.3: The comma after 'old' is incorrect because the clause is already properly set off.
